title: You’re Waiting to Feel Sorry Enough Before You Come Back to God
paragraphs: You’re Waiting to Feel Sorry Enough Before You Come Back to God
You keep thinking you need to hurt a little longer before God will let you come home. But Jesus told a story about a Father who started running while His filthy, ashamed son was still on the road.
There is a strange punishment some Christians give themselves that God never asked them to carry.
They sin.
They know they sinned.
Conviction comes.
And somewhere between conviction and repentance, shame whispers something that sounds almost holy:
Not yet.
You cannot pray yet.
You cannot worship yet.
You cannot open your Bible yet.
You cannot lift your hands yet.
You cannot call yourself close to God yet.
You need to feel worse first.
You need to prove that you really regret it.
Maybe after several miserable days...
Maybe after enough tears...
Maybe after you have punished yourself emotionally...
Maybe after you have finally become disgusted enough with what you did...
then you can come back.
And because shame can disguise itself as humility, you believe it.
So you stay away from the very Father you need most.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You have opened your Bible and felt like a hypocrite.
You have tried to pray and heard the memory of what you did louder than your own words.
You have watched other believers worship while thinking, If they knew what I did...
You have promised God things before.
You have cried before.
You have repented before.
And somehow you ended up here again.
Same temptation.
Same secret.
Same collapse.
Same sick feeling afterward.
So this time you decide you are not going to run immediately to grace.
That would feel too easy.
You think you should suffer first.
But what if the delay you are calling repentance is actually shame keeping you away from repentance?
Because biblical repentance is not convincing God to take you back.
It is turning back to the God who calls sinners to Himself.
Jesus painted this truth with devastating beauty in Luke 15.
A younger son demanded his inheritance from his father and left home. He traveled into a distant country and squandered what he had in reckless living.
Eventually everything collapsed.
The money disappeared.
A famine came.
The friends apparently disappeared with the money.
And the son who once had a place at his father's table found himself feeding pigs.
For Jesus' Jewish audience, that detail would have made the degradation especially vivid. Pigs were unclean animals under the Mosaic law.
Then Jesus gives us one of the great turning points in the parable.
Luke 15:17 begins:
“εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν...”
Eis heauton de elthōn...
Literally, the expression carries the sense of “coming to himself.”
Something broke through the madness.
The son saw where his rebellion had taken him.
He remembered his father.
He remembered home.
He decided to rise and return.
Listen carefully, because this is where many wounded believers misunderstand repentance.
The son did not sit beside the pigs waiting until he could manufacture a sufficient quantity of shame.
He got up.
That matters.
Luke 15:18 records his decision:
“ἀναστὰς πορεύσομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου...”
Anastas poreusomai pros ton patera mou...
“I will arise and go to my father.”
That is the movement shame desperately wants to prevent.
I will arise.
I will go.
Not because the far country did not matter.
Not because rebellion was harmless.
Not because sin suddenly stopped being sin.
He knew he had sinned.
He planned to confess it plainly:
“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.”
There is no excuse there.
No blame-shifting.
No pretending.
No theological vocabulary designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
He calls sin what it is.
This is not cheap grace.
This is confession.
This is repentance.
This is a sinner turning toward home.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of the story is what happens before the son can finish the speech he has rehearsed.
Jesus says:
“ἔτι δὲ αὐτοῦ μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος...”
Eti de autou makran apechontos...
“While he was still a long way off...”
His father saw him.
Please do not hurry past that.
He was still far away.
Still carrying the evidence of the far country.
Still returning from the pigs.
Still carrying his confession.
Still unable to repair everything he had destroyed.
And his father saw him.
Jesus says the father was moved with compassion.
The Greek word is powerful:
“ἐσπλαγχνίσθη”
esplanchnisthē.
It describes deep, inward compassion—a mercy felt profoundly within.
Then the father ran.
He ran toward the son.
Embraced him.
Kissed him.
And suddenly the speech the son had practiced collided with a mercy larger than the shame he had carried home.
The son confessed:
“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”
Notice something extraordinary.
Earlier, while rehearsing what he would say, the son planned to add:
“Make me like one of your hired servants.”
But in Jesus' telling, once the father reaches him, the recorded confession stops before that proposed bargain is completed.
Then the father starts giving orders.
Not instructions for punishment.
Instructions for restoration.
Bring the best robe.
Put a ring on his hand.
Put shoes on his feet.
Prepare the feast.
Celebrate.
Why?
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
Do you see what Jesus is exposing?
The son came home knowing he was unworthy.
The father did not disagree by pretending the rebellion never happened.
Instead, the father's compassion answered the returning sinner with restoration.
This does not mean every earthly consequence of sin magically disappears.

Scripture never promises that repentance eliminates every temporal consequence. Forgiveness does not always restore lost money, repair every damaged relationship overnight, erase legal consequences, or instantly rebuild broken trust.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God's mercy meeting guilty people who turn to Him.
And this is where the Gospel becomes even greater than the parable.
Because our forgiveness is not based upon God simply deciding that sin does not matter.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died for sinners.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).
And Romans 5:8 goes further:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves.
Not after we generated enough shame.
Not after we became emotionally impressive penitents.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is why repentance can never mean purchasing God's mercy with emotional suffering.
You cannot buy with tears what Jesus purchased with His blood.
Tears may accompany repentance.
Grief may accompany repentance.
In fact, Scripture speaks about godly grief producing repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).
But grief is not currency.
Feeling terrible enough does not make the cross finally become effective.
Jesus Christ is sufficient.
That is why 1 John 1:9 does not say, “If we punish ourselves long enough...”
It says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Maybe those words are difficult for you to receive because you have confused self-hatred with holiness.
You think beating yourself emotionally proves that you take sin seriously.
But there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
This is sin. Bring it into the light. Turn from it. Come to Christ.
Shame says:
You are disgusting. Hide. Stay away until you deserve to return.
One leads toward God.
The other drives you deeper into the far country.
And some of you have been living spiritually beside the pigs because you think staying miserable honors the Father more than getting up and going home.
It does not.
Your shame is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
Read that again.
Your shame is not your Savior. Jesus is.
Maybe you fell sexually.
Maybe pornography has become the secret you keep promising God you will defeat.
Maybe bitterness has been eating your heart alive.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe your marriage is carrying wounds you helped create.
Maybe you betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe alcohol, drugs, gambling, greed, envy, anger, pride, or another bondage has pulled you farther than you ever imagined you would go.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the scandal is public.
Maybe the scandal lives only between you, God, and the browser history you keep deleting.
Maybe you have become incredibly skilled at looking spiritually alive while quietly starving inside.
And every time God draws your heart toward repentance, another voice tells you:
You have done this too many times.
God must be tired of you.
You need to prove yourself first.
Stay away.
But hear Jesus' words.
The son arose.
The son went to his father.
You do not repent by running away from God until you become worthy of God.
You repent by turning from sin and returning to God because you know you are not worthy—and trusting His mercy.
That does not minimize sin.
It destroys the illusion that you can save yourself from it.
Real repentance is not saying, “What I did doesn't matter.”
Real repentance says, “What I did matters so much that I will stop defending it, stop hiding it, confess it, turn from it, and throw myself upon the mercy of God in Jesus Christ.”
That is a completely different posture.
And if your sin involves another person, repentance may require more than private tears.
You may need to tell the truth.
You may need to apologize without excuses.
You may need to make restitution where possible.
You may need accountability.
You may need to cut off access to whatever keeps pulling you back.
You may need pastoral help.
You may need to rebuild trust slowly instead of demanding that someone trust you immediately because you said sorry.
Grace does not make repentance shallow.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Because now you are no longer crawling toward God trying to negotiate the price of admission.
Christ has already paid what you could never pay.
The cross leaves no room for boasting.
And it leaves no room for despairing as though your sin were somehow more powerful than the blood of Christ.
This is the scandal of grace.
The guilty are invited home.
The unclean can be washed.
The lost can be found.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The prodigal does not rewrite his own ending.
The Father receives him.
And ultimately, the Gospel tells us that God accomplished our redemption through His Son.
Jesus Christ took the place of sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith discovers that grace is not God's reluctant tolerance of sinners who finally became impressive enough.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward people who could never rescue themselves.
So what are you waiting for?
Another night of hating yourself?
Another week avoiding prayer?
Another Sunday standing in worship while believing everyone else is allowed near Jesus except you?
How much shame would finally be enough?
Ten tears?
A hundred?
A thousand?
How many sleepless nights would purchase forgiveness?
How many days of self-loathing would equal one drop of the blood shed at Calvary?
None.
You cannot punish yourself into being forgiven.
And you do not need to crucify yourself beside Jesus as though His sacrifice needs your suffering added to it.
Repent.
Turn.
Come home.
Not tomorrow when you feel spiritual.
Now.
Confess what needs confessing.
Abandon what needs abandoning.
Repair what can be repaired.
Ask for help where you need help.
And put your confidence not in the intensity of your remorse but in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But maybe you need to stop pretending you are okay.
Your testimony might become the sentence another wounded believer needs to read tonight.
Someone on your Facebook feed may be silently convinced that they have to become worthy before God will receive them.
They may never tell you.
They may still attend church.
They may still post Bible verses.
They may still smile in photographs.
But inside, they are standing a long way from home.
There may come a night when your own heart needs these words again.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. The Gospel is too precious to keep inside the walls of people who already know it.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. It does not.
And not because God needs a transaction from you before He will bless or forgive you.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Come to Christ.
Because someday the shirts will fade.
The mugs will break.
The books will gather dust.
Facebook itself will eventually become another forgotten chapter of human technology.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps tonight, after all your running, all your hiding, all your rehearsed speeches about why you are no longer worthy...
you finally need to hear the sound Jesus placed in this story.
Footsteps.
Not yours.
The Father's.
Running toward the repentant son while he was still a long way off.
You thought you needed enough shame to begin the journey.
But shame was never the road home.
Repentance turns around. Grace meets you on the road. And Jesus is the reason home is possible.
Because maybe the most dangerous lie shame ever told you was not that you sinned.
You did.
It was that because you sinned, you should stay away from the only One who can bring you home.
